hero.headline: Second arrest made in fatal shooting of Fort Pierce art teacher Andre Barnes
hero.body:
The St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office announced a second arrest in the fatal shooting of Fort Pierce art teacher Andre Leonard Barnes, 66. Dale A. Mincey, 41, Barnes' nephew, was formally charged with first-degree murder Saturday in connection with Barnes' death. Mincey remains in custody at the St. Lucie County Jail and is being held without bond.

The fatal shooting happened July 7 at a residence on the 2700 block of Essex Drive. Deputies responded to the home at around 3:30 p.m. after receiving reports of a person with a gunshot wound. When deputies arrived, they learned a man had shot another man with a rifle. Barnes was taken to a local hospital, where he died. Karen Moye was also at the home when the shooting occurred. She heard a loud bang while she was in the bathroom and came out to find Mincey and called police, an arrest affidavit said. Moye is also facing charges in this fatal shooting, which deputies said was premeditated. Sheriff Richard Del Toro said Tuesday during a press conference that Moye, the victim's sister and mother of the suspect, knowingly provided false information to investigators and withheld pertinent information related to the homicide investigation. She has been charged with false report to law enforcement and the commission of a capital felony. Del Toro said providing false information intentionally and withholding information during a homicide investigation delays justice, diverts investigative resources, and can impact the family's ability to receive answers.

During questioning, Mincey told detectives he could not recall what happened the day of the shooting, that he did not have any issues with Barnes, and did not know how Barnes died, an arrest affidavit said. However, he admitted to owning two firearms. Moye, who lived in the home with Mincey and Barnes, told detectives immediately after the shooting that the pair did not have a good relationship and that Mincey told her he was expressing fear in the days leading up to the shooting, the arrest affidavit said. Moye told detectives Mincey said Barnes was trying to kill him and Mincey did not want to be left alone at the house. In a follow-up interview Monday, she gave a detective conflicting accounts of what happened on the day of the shooting and said she was in fear of Barnes and that something might happen between Mincey and Barnes. When asked why she didn't notify police, she said she thought both of them would get in trouble.

Barnes worked as an art teacher for the St. Lucie County School District since 2017, serving at West Gate K-8 and Samuel S. The district confirmed his passing and extended condolences to his loved ones. Barnes leaves behind three adult children. Former student Caila Coleman, who said Barnes was her 7th-grade teacher in Tallahassee, remembered him as more than just an educator. "Mr. Barnes was really a pillar of the community to us. I didn't grow up with a dad; some of my friends didn't either. We really looked at him as a father figure," Coleman said. The fatal shooting remains an active investigation and the St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office is encouraging anyone with information to contact the department or remain anonymous through Treasure Coast Crime Stoppers.

cards.headline: St. Lucie County nephew charged with murder of Fort Pierce art teacher, mother arrested for false reports
cards.body:
The St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office announced Tuesday that Dale A. Mincey, 41, has been formally charged with first-degree murder in the fatal shooting of his uncle, Andre Leonard Barnes, 66, a Fort Pierce art teacher. Mincey was arrested Saturday and remains in custody at the St. Lucie County Jail without bond. The shooting occurred July 7 at a residence on the 2700 block of Essex Drive when deputies responded around 3:30 p.m. to reports of a person with a gunshot wound. Barnes was shot with a rifle and taken to a local hospital where he died. Deputies said the fatal shooting was premeditated.

Karen Moye, Barnes' sister and Mincey's mother, was also arrested and charged with false report to law enforcement and the commission of a capital felony. Sheriff Richard Del Toro said during a Tuesday press conference that detectives uncovered information indicating Moye knowingly provided false information to investigators and withheld pertinent information related to the homicide investigation. Moye was at the home when the shooting occurred and told authorities she heard a loud bang while in the bathroom, came out to find Mincey, and called police. Del Toro said providing false information intentionally and withholding information during a homicide investigation is a serious criminal offense that delays justice, diverts investigative resources, and can impact the family's ability to receive answers.

Mincey told detectives during questioning he could not recall what happened the day of the shooting and said he did not have any issues with Barnes and did not know how Barnes died, according to an arrest affidavit. He admitted to owning two firearms. Moye, who lived in the home with both Mincey and Barnes, told detectives immediately after the shooting that the two men did not have a good relationship and that Mincey expressed fear in the days leading up to the incident, saying Barnes was trying to kill him and he did not want to be left alone at the house. In a follow-up interview Monday, Moye gave a detective conflicting accounts of what happened and told detectives she was in fear of Barnes and thought something might happen between the two men. When asked why she didn't notify police, she said she thought both of them would get in trouble and apologized for not providing complete information initially.

Barnes worked as an art teacher for the St. Lucie County School District since 2017, serving at West Gate K-8 and Samuel S. Gaines Academy. He leaves behind three adult children. Former student Caila Coleman, who said Barnes was her 7th-grade teacher in Tallahassee, remembered him as more than just an educator. "Mr. Barnes was really a pillar of the community to us. I didn't grow up with a dad; some of my friends didn't either. We really looked at him as a father figure," Coleman said. The sheriff's office said the investigation remains active and is encouraging anyone with information to contact the St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office or Treasure Coast Crime Stoppers.

cards.headline: Man fleeing ICE agents on State Road 16 struck and killed by semi truck
cards.teaser: A 28-year-old man died Tuesday after he was struck by a semi trailer truck while attempting to cross State Road 16 near a gas station after fleeing from U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents.
cards.body:
The man was one of four people who fled after an encounter between HSI and ICE agents occurred in the parking lot of a gas station. During the encounter, the four occupants of a vehicle fled on foot. One of the occupants ran across State Road 16 and into the path of the tractor trailer, according to Florida Highway Patrol officials. The pedestrian was struck by the tractor trailer in the right lane and sustained fatal injuries on scene.

Florida Highway Patrol officials confirmed they were not involved in the incident but have since opened an investigation into the death. ICE and the Department of Homeland Security have not yet commented on the incident.

The death comes as ICE is under increasing scrutiny for multiple fatal encounters. Joan Sebastian Guerrero, a 26-year-old Colombian man living in Maine, was fatally shot by ICE agents Monday during a traffic stop. Days earlier, Lorenzo Salgado Araujo was fatally wounded during a traffic stop involving ICE in Houston. The Trump administration ordered Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents to pause most traffic stops on Tuesday.

cards.headline: Gas prices in Florida jump 20 cents a gallon after Strait of Hormuz tensions
cards.teaser: Florida gas prices rose about 20 cents a gallon on Tuesday, driven by military activity in the Strait of Hormuz that pushed oil and wholesale gasoline prices higher.
cards.body:
Patrick DeHaan, a petroleum analyst with GasBuddy, said the spike is part of a broader regional trend and came in direct response to developments overseas. He said those moves were driven by the latest military activity in the Strait of Hormuz.

Jalisse Thomas, who was filling up her car in West Palm Beach, said the constant fluctuation is a financial strain. DeHaan said prices do move in both directions, but the sharp increases simply draw more attention than gradual declines. He pointed to a recent example, noting that from May 20 to June 20 of this year, gas prices dropped a dollar a gallon.

cards.headline: Palm Beach County commissioners deny private Christian school proposal in Jupiter Farms
cards.teaser: Palm Beach County commissioners voted to deny a controversial proposal to build a large private Christian school in Jupiter Farms after hours of emotional public debate over traffic, growth and the future of the community's rural character.
cards.body:
The proposal from Calvary Church would have brought a K-12 private Christian school to a vacant site on Indiantown Road, with plans for nearly 1,000 students. The issue has divided residents for months. Palm Beach County Mayor Sara Baxter was the only commissioner to vote in favor of the project, citing the need for private Christian education in the area. For more than three hours, residents lined up to speak, with traffic emerging as one of the contentious topics of the night.

One speaker told commissioners the scale of the proposed school is larger than the proposed Home Depot. Commissioners questioned whether there is actually a need for another school in the area, noting that many schools highlighted in the presentation were public schools while the proposed project would be a private school with tuition costs and different enrollment requirements. Commissioner Joel Flores pointed out that only about 25% of those who spoke in favor of the project were from Jupiter, while many supporters came from outside the area, including Port St. Lucie and Boca Raton. The county's Zoning Commission Board had already voted unanimously last month to recommend denial of the proposal. The county denied the application without prejudice, which means the school project could be brought back in a different form, but Calvary officials would have to go through the same administrative process.

cards.headline: Rising insurance costs drive Florida voters toward 2026 midterm elections, study finds
cards.teaser: The cost of homeowners insurance is becoming a key political issue in Florida, where 65 percent of respondents say rising insurance costs would make them more likely to vote in the 2026 midterms.
cards.body:
A new study from online insurance marketplace Insurify found 58 percent of Americans say rising home insurance costs are making them more likely to vote in the 2026 elections. In Florida, that number climbs to 65 percent. Insurify economist Julia Taliesin said they wanted to look at whether there was any connection in some of these states between the political environment and insurance regulation.

Insurify puts the Florida statewide average premium at $8,292, with a modest 2 percent increase expected this year. The study found 84 percent of Florida respondents plan to vote in the 2026 midterms, and 72 percent of Florida respondents are homeowners. Forty-nine percent of Florida homeowners reported their home insurance premiums increased in the last 12 months. Additionally, 57 percent of Florida respondents feel negative about the state of the economy, and 71 percent believe elections affect home insurance costs in their state. According to state leaders, reforms on insurance litigation have led to stable and in many cases lower rates, as more companies enter Florida adding to competition. Republican state leaders this year have been leading the charge for property tax reform as a new affordability target.

cards.headline: Fort Pierce residents pack planning meeting over 17-story Causeway Cove high-rise proposal
cards.body:
The Fort Pierce Planning Board reviewed the Causeway Cove development project on Monday as neighbors packed the chamber. The project, located off Seaway Drive, includes five high-rise buildings, including a 17-story building standing 192 feet tall, more than four times the city's height limit. Plans also call for two hotels and more than 70,000 square feet of retail space. The development qualifies under the Live Local Act, a state law passed in 2023 that allows developers to bypass height and density restrictions as long as they set aside 40 percent of units for affordable housing for at least 30 years. The project includes more than 900 apartments and condos, with 365 of those designated as affordable housing.

Buster Brewster, a boater at Causeway Cove Marina, said he worries the project will change the character of the area. "We're going to put this big old conglomerate up here, and I'm just afraid it's going to take away from the beauty of this place," Brewster said. Dennis Fein attended the meeting and raised concerns about traffic. "Nobody's thought this out," Fein said. "You're going to have massive traffic jams. Nobody's going to be able to get on the island, off the island." City Planning Director Kev Freeman said developers must add traffic mitigation efforts and any required intersection or access improvements. City Commissioner Michael Broderick said the city has no authority over whether the project is approved. "The city does not have a play here. We do not have a position in this. This is regulated by the state of Florida in the entirety. The city has been eliminated from the process," Broderick said. City commissioners are scheduled to hear a review of the project as the next step in the process.

hero.headline: World Cup semifinals set with England facing Argentina
hero.teaser: England and Argentina advanced to the World Cup semifinals over the weekend, joining Spain and France to complete the final four.
hero.body:
England advanced past Norway in the quarterfinals with Jude Bellingham scoring twice to inspire his team. The 23-year-old has now scored six goals in the competition, matching teammate Harry Kane for the team lead. Argentina defeated Switzerland with striker Julián Alvarez scoring in extra time to help the team through to the semifinal. The goal came with assistance from a controversial VAR call.

The four highest-ranked teams reached the semifinals despite a tournament full of underdog success stories and surprise results. England has relied on Kane and Bellingham to produce match-winning moments while looking disjointed and vulnerable at the back. The team is seeking its first World Cup title since 1966 and was last in a World Cup semifinal in 2018, when it lost to Croatia. Argentina, the defending champion, has relied on Lionel Messi and moments of brilliance to advance through the knockout rounds. The team has scored the most goals in the competition with 17. Many members of the current Argentina squad won the title in 2022. France faces Spain in one semifinal on Tuesday, while England plays Argentina on Wednesday in Atlanta. The World Cup final takes place on July 19.

cards.headline: Linda Noskova wins first Grand Slam title at Wimbledon
cards.teaser: Linda Noskova recovered from wasting five match points in the second set to defeat Karolina Muchova 6-2, 5-7, 6-3 on Saturday in an all-Czech women's final.
cards.body:
The 21-year-old Noskova became the third Czech woman in four years to win Wimbledon, following Marketa Vondrousova in 2023 and Barbora Krejcikova in 2024. Noskova overcame a second-set meltdown in which she wasted five match points before securing her first Grand Slam trophy.

Petra Kvitova, who won Wimbledon in 2011 and 2014, was in attendance. Martina Navratilova, who won a record nine singles titles at the All England Club, looked on from the Royal Box, where she was seated next to Kate, the Princess of Wales. Kate presented the Venus Rosewater Dish trophy to Noskova.

Muchova and Noskova played doubles together at the 2024 Paris Olympics and finished fourth. The victory established Noskova as the latest in a long line of Czech women to win the grass-court major championship.

cards.headline: Jannik Sinner beats Alexander Zverev to defend Wimbledon title
cards.teaser: Top-ranked Jannik Sinner defeated Alexander Zverev 6-7, 7-6, 6-3, 6-4 on Sunday for his second consecutive Wimbledon championship and fifth Grand Slam title.
cards.body:
Jannik Sinner beat Alexander Zverev 6-7 (7), 7-6 (2), 6-3, 6-4 Sunday for his second consecutive title at the All England Club and his fifth Grand Slam title. The top-ranked Italian ripped a forehand winner up the line on his first match point and dropped to the grass on his back in celebration. The victory came in his first tournament since a second-round meltdown at the French Open, when he wilted in a Paris heat wave and had his 30-match winning streak ended after coming within one game of a straight-set victory over Juan Manuel Cerundolo, who was ranked No. 56. A year ago, Sinner beat Carlos Alcaraz in the final at the All England Club after wasting three match points against his rival in the Roland Garros final. Prince William joined his wife Kate and two of their children for the final in a star-studded Royal Box that also included actors Dustin Hoffman, Nicole Kidman and Ben Stiller.

The top two seeds appeared perfectly matched until Zverev earned his first break point of the match at 3-3 in the third set, 2 hours and 42 minutes in. Sinner produced a drop shot and Zverev slipped and appeared to hyperextend his right knee as he attempted to change directions behind the baseline. Sinner went around the net and helped his opponent up off the grass. Zverev quickly resumed playing but appeared slightly hampered and slung his racket across the baseline in frustration when he missed a forehand and handed Sinner the first break of the match and a 5-3 lead in the third. It was Sinner's 10th straight victory over Zverev, who was coming off his first Grand Slam title at the French Open.

hero.headline: Florida Democrats claim special-election momentum ahead of 2026 legislative races
hero.body:
Florida Democratic Party Chair Nikki Fried said during a virtual briefing Monday that the Republican supermajority in the legislature is breakable and Democrats are going to break it this cycle. The party pointed to more than 30 local and special-election flips since the 2024 election, more than 3,000 volunteers, increased candidate recruitment and an advantage in requests for vote-by-mail ballots. The party's tally includes local offices as well as recent legislative special elections, not 30 seats in the Florida Legislature. Fried said the difference this cycle is the party's Pendulum Project, a year-round organizing operation designed to maintain voter contact between major elections. Democrats are building their message around affordability, blaming nearly three decades of Republican control for rising housing, property-insurance, healthcare and everyday living costs. Party leaders said they will challenge a Republican-backed property-tax amendment headed to voters, arguing that cutting local-government revenue could threaten services or shift costs elsewhere.

Republicans remain at or above the two-thirds threshold needed for supermajority power in both legislative chambers. A two-thirds majority amounts to 80 of the 120 House seats and 27 of the 40 Senate seats when every member is present. As of May 31, Florida had about 5.54 million active registered Republicans and 4.03 million Democrats, according to the state Division of Elections. Another 3.32 million voters were registered without a party affiliation. Democrats will continue making their case at Leadership Blue, the state party's annual gathering, scheduled for July 17 through 19 at Disney's Coronado Springs Resort in Lake Buena Vista. Former Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg will deliver the keynote address at the July 18 gala.

hero.headline: Martin County faces $2.1 billion transportation funding gap with nine road widening projects unfunded
hero.teaser: Martin County will need approximately $2.8 billion for transportation improvements over the next 20 years but only $701 million is currently available, leaving nine identified road widening projects without funding.
hero.body:
Martin County faces a $2.1 billion transportation funding shortfall over the next two decades, with nine road widening projects left without financial backing, according to a PowerPoint obtained through a public records request. The Martin County Metropolitan Planning Organization estimates the county will need approximately $2.8 billion for transportation improvements over the next 20 years, but only $701 million is currently available. This means the county can fund just about one quarter of its identified transportation needs.

Beth Beltran, administrator for Martin County's Metropolitan Planning Organization, said the cost analysis was emailed to county and Stuart officials last August. Of the $701 million currently available, all but $10 million comes from state and federal funding sources. The significant funding gap has forced difficult decisions about which transportation projects can move forward and which must remain on hold.

Among the most pressing unfunded needs are nine roads the county identified as requiring widening as traffic grows. The total cost to widen those roads is approximately $213 million, money that is not currently available, leaving all nine projects out of the county's draft Cost Feasible Plan. Those roads include SW Martin Downs Boulevard, SR-714/SW Martin Highway, SW 96th Street, SW Bridge Road, CR-714/SW Martin Highway, SW Allapattah Road/CR-609, SE Green River Parkway, SW Indiantown Avenue, and SE Bridge Road/CR-708.

State Road 710 is among the county's highest priorities due to safety concerns. Beltran said fatal crashes as well as serious injury crashes were just enormous on that corridor, with improvements estimated at about $300 million. The substantial price tag for State Road 710 alone represents nearly half of the total funding shortfall and highlights the challenge facing county officials as they balance safety needs against available resources. The funding gap affects not just road widening projects but a range of transportation improvements needed across the county over the next two decades.

cards.headline: Port St. Lucie Opens Registration for Free City University Program
cards.teaser:
Registration is now open for Port St. Lucie City University, a free nine-session program designed to help residents better understand how their local government operates.

Classes
cards.body:
Registration is now open for Port St. Lucie City University, a free nine-session program designed to help residents better understand how their local government operates.

Classes begin Wednesday, Aug. 12, and will be held from **5:30 to 8:30 p.m. in the Council Chambers at Port St. Lucie City Hall**, located at 121 SW Port St. Lucie Blvd.

Participants will learn about City departments, municipal services and the decision-making processes that shape the community. The program also gives residents opportunities to meet City staff, ask questions and gain a closer look at the work involved in operating one of Florida's largest cities.

Residents who complete the course will receive a certificate of completion and may also choose to become a City Ambassador, helping share information about City programs and services throughout the community.

City University is intended to encourage civic engagement while strengthening connections between residents and local government. Since the program began in 2016, more than 600 residents have participated.

**Enrollment is limited to 160 participants.**

Residents who are unable to attend the in-person classes can also access City U on Demand, which offers a more flexible way to learn about Port St. Lucie government and municipal operations.

hero.headline: Jupiter Inlet Lighthouse offers 165 years of history with 105-step climb to panoramic views
hero.teaser: The Jupiter Inlet Lighthouse, built in 1860, offers visitors a 105-step climb to panoramic views of the Atlantic Ocean, Jupiter Inlet, and Loxahatchee and Indian rivers.
hero.body:
The Jupiter Inlet Lighthouse, a red brick tower constructed in 1860 at the base of the Jupiter Inlet on Florida's Atlantic coast, has operated continuously for 165 years as both an active navigational aid and a public attraction. The historic structure has guided mariners since before the Civil War while welcoming visitors who climb to its observation gallery for sweeping views of the surrounding waterways and coastline. Modern visitors follow the same path that lighthouse keepers took throughout history to maintain operations, ascending 105 steps up a narrow spiral staircase that winds through the interior of the brick tower to reach the observation gallery at the top.

The spiral staircase follows the route that lighthouse keepers climbed night after night to maintain the powerful Fresnel lens that projected light across the water to passing ships. This path leads upward through the tower to the gallery, allowing visitors to retrace the steps of the early keepers who ensured the beacon remained operational throughout the decades. The climb through the narrow staircase provides a tangible connection to the daily work of the keepers who operated this station across more than a century and a half of continuous service.

The observation gallery at the top provides panoramic views stretching across multiple waterways and the ocean. The Atlantic Ocean extends to the east, while below the tower, the turquoise waters of the Jupiter Inlet converge with the Loxahatchee and Indian rivers. Visitors at this elevated vantage point can watch boats glide through the channel as sea breezes sweep across the observation area. The commanding perspective reveals why this location proved ideal for a lighthouse, offering clear sightlines across the coastal landscape and waterways that allowed keepers to monitor maritime traffic and project the beacon across miles of ocean.

The museum grounds preserve more than just the tower itself. Restored historic buildings chronicle the lighthouse's journey from its construction before the Civil War through its years as an active Coast Guard station. These structures provide information about the lighthouse's role in regional maritime history and offer details about the daily lives of the keepers who operated the station. The site maintains the supporting buildings that allowed the lighthouse station to function across generations, preserving the complete story of this working navigational aid that has marked the Florida coastline for mariners throughout its 165 years of operation.
